english: I'd like to open an account
usage: 계좌 만들고 싶어요
I'd like to open an account
Polite 존댓말, the everyday opening line at the bank counter
계좌 개설하려고요
I'm here to open an account
개설하다 is the formal/bank-form verb for 'open (an account)'; mirrors the teller's own register
통장 만들러 왔어요
I came to open a bankbook
통장 (passbook) is what people say casually for a basic account; slightly more colloquial
계좌 하나 만들려고 하는데요
I'm looking to open an account
-는데요 softens the request and invites the teller to guide you next
examples: 계좌 만들고 싶어요.
I'd like to open an account.
Said to the teller as you sit down; the simplest, safest opener with any bank staff
A: 어떻게 오셨어요? / B: 계좌 만들고 싶어요. 외국인인데 어떤 서류 필요해요?
A: How can I help you? / B: I'd like to open an account. I'm a foreigner — what documents do I need?
Real two-turn exchange: state your purpose then immediately flag 외국인 status so the teller tells you what's required
월급 받을 계좌 하나 개설하려고 왔는데요.
I came to open an account to receive my salary.
State the purpose (월급 받을 'to receive a salary'); banks sometimes ask why, and giving a reason speeds things up
nuance: 계좌 만들고 싶어요 is 계좌 (計座, 'account') + 만들다 ('to make') + -고 싶어요 ('I want to'): the plain spoken way to tell a teller you want to open an account. Two nouns are in play: 계좌 is the technical term — the account number used on forms, apps, and bank systems — while 통장 literally means the physical passbook but in everyday speech doubles as 'account' (so 통장 만들고 싶어요 sounds just as natural and a bit more colloquial). The bank's own paperwork and staff prefer the verb 개설하다 ('to establish/open'), so mirroring that verb in 계좌 개설하려고요 puts you on the right register. For a salary account specifically, say 급여 계좌 만들고 싶어요. The English-speaker trap is translating 'open' literally as 열다 ('to open a door') — 계좌 열고 싶어요 is wrong; an account is 만들다 or 개설하다, never 열다. This phrase is always addressed to staff, so 존댓말 is the only appropriate register here.

structuredNuance.t: 계좌 (計座, 'account') + 만들다 ('to make') + -고 싶어요 ('I want to'). The verb is 만들다 — you literally 'make' an account, not 'open' one as in English. For a salary account say 급여 계좌 만들고 싶어요; for an account to receive transfers say 입금 받을 계좌요.

계좌 만들다 (plain speech) ≈ 계좌 개설하다 (formal, bank's own verb, better on paperwork). 통장 만들다 is the colloquial alternative — 통장 is the physical passbook but stands in for 'account' in casual talk. Choose 개설하다 at the counter for polish.
계좌 is Sino-Korean 計座, 'reckoning-seat → account'. 개설 is 開設, 'open + establish', the formal banking term.
Always addressed to bank staff, so 존댓말 is required. No 반말 version is appropriate here. You can soften with -려고 하는데요 to invite the teller to guide you, or be direct with 만들고 싶어요.

Saying 계좌 열고 싶어요 — 열다 means 'to open a door/lid/shop', never a bank account. An account is 만들다 (make) or 개설하다 (establish). Calquing 'open an account' word-for-word is the single most common error here.

mistakes: Saying 계좌 열고 싶어요.
열다 ('to open') is for doors, lids, or shops — not bank accounts. You MAKE an account: 계좌 만들고 싶어요, or formally 계좌 개설하려고요.
Confusing 계좌 with 계산.
계좌 is a bank account; 계산 is 'calculation / paying a bill'. They sound close but 계산하고 싶어요 would mean 'I want to pay', not 'open an account'.
Using 통장 to mean the account number.
통장 is the physical passbook (and casually 'account'); the account NUMBER is 계좌번호. To give your number, say 계좌번호, not 통장.

english: I'd like to check my balance
usage: 잔액 확인하고 싶어요
I'd like to check my balance
Polite; said to a teller or narrated aloud before using an ATM
잔액 조회 좀 할게요
Let me check the balance
조회 ('inquiry/lookup') is the exact button label on ATMs and banking apps
통장 잔고가 얼마예요?
How much is in my account?
잔고 is the casual everyday synonym for 'balance' in spoken Korean
잔액이 얼마 남았어요?
How much balance is left?
남다 ('to remain') framing — very natural in conversational speech
examples: 잔액 확인하고 싶어요.
I'd like to check my balance.
Said to a teller, or aloud to yourself before deciding whether to withdraw
A: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요. / B: 네, 잔액 조회해 드릴게요. 잠깐만요.
A: Please check if the deposit came in. / B: Of course, let me look up the balance for you. Just a moment.
Two-turn exchange: customer requests balance check using 잔액 조회, the official ATM/app term the teller mirrors back
이체하기 전에 잔액부터 확인할게요.
Before transferring, let me check the balance first.
잔액부터 ('starting with the balance') — 부터 = 'starting from/first'; confirms you have enough before sending
nuance: 잔액 확인하고 싶어요 is 잔액 (殘額, 'remaining amount = balance') + 확인하다 ('to check/confirm') + -고 싶어요. Two near-synonyms matter: 잔액 is the formal term printed on receipts, ATM menus, and statements, while 잔고 ('balance / what's left') is the warmer everyday word in casual speech ('통장에 잔고가 없어' = 'my account's empty'). On machines and in apps, the action is labeled 잔액 조회 ('balance inquiry'), where 조회 specifically means looking up stored information — so 조회 is the word you tap, and 확인 is the broader 'check/confirm' you say aloud. The particle trap: it's 잔액을 확인하다 (object particle 을), not 잔액에 확인하다 (location particle 에). To a teller use polite speech; with a friend drop to 잔고 얼마야? The English-speaker trap is reaching for 균형 ('equilibrium, physical balance') for a bank balance — 통장 균형 is meaningless to Koreans; the bank term is 잔액 or 잔고 only.

structuredNuance.t: 잔액 (殘額, 'remaining amount') + 확인하다 ('to verify/confirm') + -고 싶어요. 잔액 is formally 'the amount remaining', which is exactly what a bank balance is. With a teller use 잔액 확인; with a friend say 잔고 얼마야? The particle is 을: 잔액을 확인하다.

잔액 (formal, on receipts/ATMs) vs 잔고 (warmer casual, in chat: 잔고 없어). 확인하다 ('confirm/check') vs 조회하다 ('look up in a system') — 잔액 조회 is the ATM button; 잔액 확인 is what you say aloud. They overlap but 조회 is screen/app language.
잔액 is 殘額, '殘 remaining + 額 amount'. The partner term 잔고 (殘高) shares 殘 but uses 高 ('height/level') — both mean 'remaining balance' but at different registers.

Polite 존댓말 with any teller or ATM-screen context. Drop to 잔고 얼마야? with close friends checking their own account. This phrase would be odd in 반말 since you're always either speaking to staff or narrating to yourself.

Translating 'balance' as 균형 — 균형 is physical/abstract equilibrium ('keep your balance'). A bank balance is 잔액 (formal) or 잔고 (casual). Also watch the particle: 잔액을 확인하다 (object 을), not 잔액에 확인하다 (location 에 doesn't fit here).

mistakes: Translating 'balance' as 균형.
균형 is physical/abstract equilibrium ('keep your balance'). A bank balance is 잔액 (formal) or 잔고 (casual). 통장 균형 is meaningless to Koreans.
Saying 잔액에 확인하고 싶어요.
확인하다 takes the object particle 을/를: 잔액을 확인하고 싶어요. The particle 에 (location/time) is wrong here.
Mixing up 조회 and 충전.
조회 is 'inquiry/look up' (checking the balance); 충전 is 'top up/recharge' (adding money, e.g. to a transit card). Tap 조회 to SEE the balance, not 충전.

english: I'm going to withdraw some cash
usage: 현금 좀 뽑으려고요
I'm going to take out some cash
Casual-polite; 뽑다 ('pull out') is the everyday verb specifically for ATM cash
출금하려고 하는데요
I'd like to make a withdrawal
출금 (出金) is the formal/screen word for 'withdrawal' — closer to what you say at a counter
돈 좀 찾으려고요
I'm going to withdraw some money
찾다 (lit. 'find/retrieve') is the standard neutral verb for getting your money out
오만 원만 뽑을게요
I'll just take out 50,000 won
Stating the amount upfront; 만 ('only/just') limits it
examples: 현금 좀 뽑으려고요.
I'm going to take out some cash.
Said heading to the ATM, or telling a friend why you're stopping
A: 잠깐만요, 현금 좀 뽑고 올게요. / B: 아, ATM 저기 있어요.
A: Just a moment — I'll go take out some cash and be right back. / B: Oh, the ATM is right over there.
A/B exchange: natural pre-errand announcement; B points you to the machine
통장에서 십만 원 찾고 싶은데요.
I'd like to withdraw 100,000 won from my account.
통장에서 ('from the account') — source takes 에서; 찾다 is the standard polite counter verb
nuance: 현금 좀 뽑으려고요 is 현금 (現金, 'cash') + 좀 (softener) + 뽑다 ('to pull/draw out') + -으려고요 ('I intend to'). Korean has three verbs for getting money out, and choosing right matters: 뽑다 is the breezy spoken verb for pulling cash from an ATM (돈 뽑다 = 'hit the ATM'); 찾다 — which elsewhere means 'find' — is the neutral standard 'withdraw' used at a counter or machine (돈을 찾다); and 출금하다 (出金) is the formal Sino-Korean word on screens and forms. The opposite — depositing — is 입금하다 or 넣다; keep 출금 (money out) vs 입금 (money in) firmly apart, since swapping them at a teller causes real mistakes. With a friend you'd say 돈 좀 뽑을게. The English-speaker traps: calquing 'withdraw' as 철수하다 (military 'retreat') is wrong; and the word 찾다 in a banking context means 'withdraw', not 'look for' — 돈 찾으러 가요 = 'going to withdraw money', not 'going to search for it'.

structuredNuance.t: 현금 (現金, 'cash') + 좀 (softener) + 뽑다 ('to pull out') + -으려고요 ('I intend to'). 뽑다 is colloquial for ATM cash; the neutral verb for any withdrawal context is 찾다. Formal on forms and screens: 출금하다. With friends: 돈 좀 뽑을게.

뽑다 ('pull out', breezy/ATM-specific) vs 찾다 ('retrieve', neutral, counter or ATM) vs 출금하다 (出金, formal Sino-Korean on screens). Opposite: 입금하다 / 넣다 (deposit). 뽑다 sounds casual and vivid; 출금 is the official term.
현금 is 現金 ('cash'); 출금 is 出金 ('money out', formal withdrawal); 입금 is 入金 ('money in', deposit). The 出/入 pairing is the key to remembering which way money moves.
현금 좀 뽑으려고요 is casual-polite — fine with a colleague or when talking out loud. At a counter use 출금하려고 하는데요 or 돈 찾고 싶어요. With friends just say 돈 뽑을게. Never use 반말 with bank staff.

Two traps: (1) calquing 'withdraw' as 철수하다 — 철수 is military/strategic withdrawal (retreat), not money. (2) 찾다 in banking means 'retrieve/withdraw', not 'look for' — 돈 찾으러 가요 = going to withdraw, not going on a treasure hunt.

mistakes: Translating 'withdraw' as 철수하다 or 후퇴하다.
Those mean military/strategic withdrawal (retreat). For money it's 출금하다 / 돈을 찾다 / 돈을 뽑다.
Reading 돈 찾다 as 'look for money'.
In a banking context 찾다 means 'withdraw' (retrieve your money), not 'search'. 돈 찾으러 왔어요 = 'I came to withdraw money'.
Confusing 출금 and 입금.
출금 (出金) = money OUT (withdrawal); 입금 (入金) = money IN (deposit). Tell the teller 출금이요 to take cash out, 입금이요 to put money in.

usage: 수수료 있어요?
Is there a fee?
Polite-neutral; the basic question before any transaction — ATM, transfer, exchange
수수료 얼마예요?
How much is the fee?
When you already expect a fee and want the exact amount
수수료 안 붙어요?
No fee gets charged?
붙다 ('to be attached') is how Koreans say a fee is 'added on' — very idiomatic
수수료 면제돼요?
Is the fee waived?
면제되다 ('to be exempted') — asking if you qualify for free service
examples: 수수료 있어요?
Is there a fee?
Asked before transferring money or using another bank's ATM
A: 다른 은행 ATM이라 수수료 붙어요? / B: 네, 800원 붙어요.
A: It's another bank's ATM — will a fee get charged? / B: Yes, 800 won gets added.
A/B exchange: the natural 붙다 verb in both question and answer — fee 'attaches' to the transaction
이체 수수료는 면제고, 출금만 수수료 있어요.
Transfer fees are waived; only withdrawals have a fee.
Hear the teller distinguish 이체 vs 출금 fees; 면제 = exemption
nuance: 수수료 있어요? is 수수료 (手數料, 'handling fee/commission') + 있어요? ('is there?'). 수수료 is the all-purpose word for a bank transaction fee — ATM fees, transfer fees, wire fees, exchange margins — making it the single most useful money word for navigating a Korean bank. The most idiomatic verb pairing is 붙다 ('to stick/attach'): Koreans say 수수료가 붙어요 ('a fee gets tacked on'), which sounds more natural than the textbook 수수료를 내다 ('to pay a fee'); both are correct, but 붙다 describes fees that appear automatically on a transaction. To ask about a fee waiver, use 면제되다: 수수료 면제돼요? The key dividing line from 요금: 요금 is a fare or utility charge (전기 요금, 택시 요금), while 수수료 is the bank's cut for handling your transaction. Don't ask a bank about 요금. The English-speaker trap is using 비용 or 가격 — too generic and off-register for a bank fee. Grammar note: 붙다 is intransitive, so the subject particle is 가: 수수료가 붙어요, not 수수료를 붙어요.

structuredNuance.t: 수수료 (手數料, 'handling fee/commission') + 있어요? ('is there?'). 수수료 covers all transaction fees at a bank: ATM, wire, exchange margin. The idiom: 수수료가 붙어요 ('a fee attaches/is added') — 붙다 is intransitive so the subject takes 가, never 를.

수수료 (bank/transaction fee, handling cut) vs 요금 (fare/utility charge: 택시 요금, 전기 요금). Ask 수수료 있어요? at a bank; ask 요금 얼마예요? for a cab or utility bill. Also: 수수료를 내다 (pay a fee, textbook) vs 수수료가 붙다 (fee attaches, idiomatic spoken).
수수료 is 手數料 — 手數 'the number of hand-moves (labor)' + 料 'charge'. A fee for the work of handling your transaction.

Used with tellers, ATMs, and exchange booths — always 존댓말. The question mark structure stays the same in casual speech (수수료 있어?) when talking to a friend about their bank, but you'd still use 있어요? with any staff.
Using 비용 ('cost/expense') or 가격 ('price') for a bank fee — both are too generic. The specific word is 수수료. Also: 붙다 is intransitive — 수수료가 붙어요 (subject 가), not 수수료를 붙어요 (object 를 is wrong here).

mistakes: Using 요금 for a bank transaction fee.
요금 is a fare/utility charge (택시 요금, 전기 요금). A bank's handling fee is 수수료: 송금 수수료, 출금 수수료.
Saying 가격 or 비용 for the fee.
가격 is the 'price' of a product; 비용 is general 'cost/expense'. The specific banking word is 수수료. Ask 수수료 얼마예요?, not 가격 얼마예요?.
Saying 수수료를 붙어요.
붙다 ('to be attached') is intransitive — the fee attaches itself: 수수료가 붙어요 (subject 가). With an object particle it'd be the transitive 붙이다. Use 수수료가 붙어요.

usage: 비밀번호 입력해 주세요
Please enter your PIN
What the teller or machine says TO you; 입력하다 = 'input' (formal screen term)
비밀번호 눌러 주세요
Please key in your password
눌러 주세요 ('please press') — common spoken version a counter teller uses
비밀번호 네 자리요
Four-digit PIN
자리 = 'digit/place'; Korean card PINs are almost always 네 자리 (4 digits)
비밀번호 잊어버렸어요
I forgot my password
What YOU say when you can't remember it — the situation is now reversed
examples: 비밀번호 입력해 주세요.
Please enter your PIN.
The teller slides the keypad toward you and says this — it's directed at the customer
A: 비밀번호 네 자리 눌러 주세요. / B: 네. (누름) 됐어요?
A: Please key in your 4-digit PIN. / B: Sure. (presses) Is that it?
A/B counter exchange: teller requests, customer confirms — 됐어요? = 'is that done?'
비밀번호 세 번 틀려서 카드가 잠겼어요.
I got the PIN wrong 3 times so my card got locked.
세 번 틀리다 ('wrong 3 times') triggers the standard lockout; explain this to the teller so they can unlock it
nuance: 비밀번호 (秘密番號, lit. 'secret number') covers PIN, app password, and even door code — Korean does not split 'PIN' from 'password' the way English does. The same word serves your card PIN at the ATM, your banking app login, and the gym locker code. Two verbs go with it: 입력하다 ('to input', the formal screen word) and 누르다 ('to press', the spoken 'key it in'); 비밀번호 입력해 주세요 and 비밀번호 눌러 주세요 are interchangeable, the latter slightly warmer. This phrase is usually said TO you by staff or the machine — the honorific 주세요 makes it a polite request to the customer; when YOU forgot it you flip to 비밀번호 잊어버렸어요. Digit count uses 자리 ('place/digit'): 네 자리 = four digits. The English-speaker traps: calling it 패스워드 sounds IT/tech-only; using 암호 sounds like a spy cipher or encryption, not a bank PIN. Also don't confuse 비밀번호 (secret, never share) with 계좌번호 (account number, freely shared to receive money).

structuredNuance.t: 비밀번호 (秘密番號, 'secret number') covers PIN, app password, and door code — Korean has one word for all. This phrase is usually said TO you by staff (주세요 = polite request to the customer). When YOU forgot it: 비밀번호 잊어버렸어요. Digits: 네 자리 = 4-digit PIN.
비밀번호 입력해 주세요 (formal, screen/teller) vs 비밀번호 눌러 주세요 (spoken, slightly warmer). Don't confuse 비밀번호 (secret PIN, never share) with 계좌번호 (account number, share freely to get paid).
비밀번호 is 秘密番號 — 秘密 'secret' + 番號 'number'. The bundling of PIN and password into one word reflects that Korean security culture uses one term for all personal access codes.

Always 존댓말 in a bank/ATM/shop context — you're speaking to or being addressed by staff. The phrase 비밀번호 입력해 주세요 is directed AT the customer (they are the subject of 'entering'). In casual tech talk 비번 is the shortened form (비밀번호 → 비번).

Using 패스워드 (tech-only loanword) or 암호 ('cipher/secret code' — sounds like spy terminology). The universal daily-life word is 비밀번호. Also: mixing up 비밀번호 with 계좌번호 is a genuine security slip — never give your 비밀번호 to receive money.

mistakes: Confusing 비밀번호 with 계좌번호.
비밀번호 is your SECRET PIN/password (never share it); 계좌번호 is your account NUMBER (you give it out to receive money). Mixing them is a real security slip.
Using 암호 for a bank PIN.
암호 leans toward 'cipher/secret code/encryption'. Your everyday card PIN and app login are 비밀번호. Banks and ATMs all say 비밀번호.
Saying 비밀번호를 눌러요 to staff as a request.
As a polite request TO the customer it needs the favor form: 비밀번호 눌러 주세요 / 입력해 주세요. Bare 눌러요 sounds like a flat statement, not a courteous instruction.

english: I'd like to send money here
usage: 여기로 송금하고 싶어요
I'd like to send money here
Polite; 송금 (送金) is the formal word for 'remittance'; 여기로 marks the destination with 로
이 계좌로 돈 보내고 싶어요
I want to send money to this account
보내다 ('to send') is the plain everyday verb; account takes 로
계좌이체 좀 하려고요
I'd like to do a bank transfer
계좌이체 = account-to-account electronic transfer (the standard app/ATM method)
해외로 송금돼요?
Can I send money overseas?
해외 송금 = international remittance; ask if your account/bank supports it
examples: 여기로 송금하고 싶어요.
I'd like to send money here.
Handing over a slip with the account details to the teller
A: 이 계좌로 삼십만 원 보내 주실 수 있어요? / B: 네, 계좌번호랑 예금주 성함 확인해 드릴게요.
A: Could you send 300,000 won to this account? / B: Sure, let me confirm the account number and account holder's name.
Full counter exchange: 이 계좌로 ('to this account', destination takes 로); teller cross-checks 예금주 name
미국에 있는 가족한테 송금하려고 하는데요.
I'm trying to send money to family in the US.
가족한테 ('to family') — person takes 한테; 미국에 marks the location; use 하는데요 to invite guidance
nuance: 여기로 송금하고 싶어요 uses 송금 (送金, 'send-money = remittance') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. Three terms cluster here: 송금 is the formal umbrella for sending money to someone (especially overseas wire transfers, 해외 송금); 계좌이체 (or just 이체) is specifically account-to-account electronic transfer done via app or ATM; 보내다 ('to send') is the plain casual verb. For a teller, either 송금하고 싶어요 or 이체하고 싶어요 works. The make-or-break point is particles for the destination: an account/bank/place takes 로/으로 — 이 계좌로 보내다; a PERSON takes 한테/에게 — 친구한테 송금하다. English speakers overuse 에 here: 이 계좌에 보내다 sounds unnatural to Koreans; native is 이 계좌로. Also keep 송금 (sending OUT) apart from 입금 (money coming IN): if you want to receive money, share your 계좌번호 so someone else can 입금/송금 to you. Don't translate 'transfer' as 옮기다 — that means physically moving objects.

structuredNuance.t: 송금 (送金, 'send-money') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. 송금 is the formal term, especially for overseas remittance. Destination particle rule: place/account takes 로 (이 계좌로); person takes 한테/에게 (친구한테). Either 송금 or 이체 is natural with a teller.

송금 (formal umbrella, esp. overseas) vs 계좌이체/이체 (account-to-account, in-app/ATM) vs 보내다 (casual spoken). Also: 송금 = outgoing (you send); 입금 = incoming (money arrives). They're opposite sides of the same transfer.
송금 is 送金, '送 send + 金 money'. 해외 송금 (海外送金) = overseas remittance. The partner term 입금 is 入金, 'money coming in'.

Always 존댓말 at a bank counter. In a banking app you tap through menus, but when you speak or message about it use the same polite forms. With friends texting 돈 보낼게 is casual and natural — no need for 송금 in casual chat.

Two traps: (1) using 에 for the destination account — native Korean is 이 계좌로 (direction particle 로), not 이 계좌에. (2) Translating 'transfer' as 옮기다 ('to move/relocate an object') — money transfer is 이체/송금, never 옮기다.

mistakes: Marking the destination account with 에 instead of 로.
Money goes TO an account with 로/으로: 이 계좌로 보내 주세요. 이 계좌에 보내다 sounds unnatural to natives.
Using 한테/에게 for an account number.
한테/에게 are for PEOPLE (친구한테 송금). An account or bank takes 로/으로 (이 계좌로). Match the particle to person vs. thing.
Translating 'transfer' as 옮기다.
옮기다 means physically moving/relocating something. A money transfer is 이체하다 or 송금하다. 돈을 옮기다 sounds like carrying cash around.

usage: 이체할게요
I'll make a transfer
Polite; announcing your own intended action with -ㄹ게요
계좌이체로 할게요
I'll pay by bank transfer
Choosing transfer as the payment method over card or cash
이체했어요
I've made the transfer / I sent it
Past tense — telling someone the money has been sent on your side
바로 이체해 드릴게요
I'll transfer it to you right away
-아/어 드리다 (humble favor form) when sending to someone you respect
examples: 이체할게요.
I'll make the transfer.
Said at the counter or aloud as you confirm in the banking app
A: 현금 없어서 계좌이체로 할게요. / B: 계좌번호 알려 주세요.
A: I have no cash so I'll pay by bank transfer. / B: Please give me your account number.
Classic split-the-bill exchange: 계좌이체로 할게요 is the payment choice; B responds with the natural 계좌번호 알려 주세요
방금 이체했는데 입금됐는지 확인 좀 해 주세요.
I just transferred it — please check if it arrived.
이체했다 (you sent) vs 입금됐다 (it landed on their end) — two different verbs for the same money moving
nuance: 이체할게요 is 이체 (移替, 'account-to-account transfer') + -할게요, the -ㄹ게요 ending that announces your own intended action politely. 이체 is the precise word for moving money electronically between accounts; 계좌이체 spells it out fully and is the label for 'pay by bank transfer' as a payment method — standard in Korea for rent, large purchases, and splitting bills. The everyday alternative is 보내다 ('send'), so 돈 보낼게요 and 이체할게요 mean the same in casual use, with 이체 sounding a touch more official. The crucial paired vocabulary: when you've SENT money you say 이체했어요 (active, you transferred), but confirming it ARRIVED uses 입금됐어요? (passive, deposited on their side) — the two verbs describe the same money from opposite perspectives. The English-speaker trap is register: 이체할게요 is natural conversational speech; 이체하겠습니다 is stiff/overly formal for everyday use. To send to someone senior, add the humble 드리다: 이체해 드릴게요. Don't confuse 이체 with 환전 (currency exchange).

structuredNuance.t: 이체 (移替, 'move-replace = account transfer') + -할게요 ('I will/intend to', speaker-side announcement). -ㄹ게요 signals your own decision; it's different from -겠어요 (more formal intent/presumption). 계좌이체 = the full compound used as a payment method label.

이체하다 ('transfer electronically', precise) vs 보내다 ('send', casual) vs 송금하다 (formal, esp. overseas). Crucial pair: 이체했어요 (I sent — your action) vs 입금됐어요 (it arrived — their side, passive). Don't swap them.
이체 is 移替 — 移 'move' + 替 'replace/switch'. The money moves and the ownership switches. Compare 환전 (換錢, 'swap-money'), which is a currency exchange, not an account transfer.

이체할게요 is natural polite speech at a counter or in chat. Upgrade to 이체해 드릴게요 (humble -드리다) when sending money to someone senior. Don't use 이체하겠습니다 casually — that -겠습니다 sounds unnatural in everyday situations.

Over-formalizing as 이체하겠습니다 in casual settings — 이체할게요 is the natural polite form. Also confusing 이체 (account transfer) with 환전 (currency exchange) — entirely different transactions. And mixing up 이체했어요 (I sent) with 입금됐어요 (it arrived).

mistakes: Saying 이체했어요 to mean the recipient got it.
이체했어요 means YOU sent it. Whether it ARRIVED is 입금됐어요? (deposited on their end). The two sides have different verbs: 이체 (send) vs 입금 (receive).
Over-formalizing as 이체하겠습니다 in casual settings.
합쇼체 sounds stiff for an everyday transfer. The natural polite form is 이체할게요. Save 하겠습니다 for formal/business contexts.
Confusing 이체 with 환전.
이체 (移替) is account-to-account transfer; 환전 (換錢) is exchanging currency. Don't say 이체 when you mean to swap dollars for won.

english: Could you give me your account number?
usage: 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요
Could you give me your account number?
Polite; asking someone for their account details so you can pay them
계좌번호 불러 주세요
Please read out your account number
불러 주세요 ('read it aloud') when you'll type as they dictate
계좌 하나 찍어 주세요
Send me your account info
찍어 주세요 — casual 'shoot me' the account details (text it over)
제 계좌번호 알려 드릴게요
I'll give you my account number
The reverse: humbly giving YOURS to someone; -드리다 for humility
examples: 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요.
Could you give me your account number?
Asking a friend so you can send your share after splitting a meal
A: 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요. / B: 국민은행이요, 0123-45-6789예요. 예금주는 김민준이에요.
A: Could you give me your account number? / B: It's Kookmin Bank, 0123-45-6789. Account holder is Kim Min-jun.
Full real exchange: B gives bank name first, then number, then 예금주 (holder) — the complete info needed to transfer
계좌번호랑 예금주 성함 좀 알려 주세요.
Please tell me the account number and the holder's name.
예금주 ('account holder') name is checked by the banking app before you can confirm a transfer
nuance: 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요 is 계좌번호 ('account number') + 좀 (softener) + 알려 주세요 ('please let me know', from 알리다 'to inform' + 주다 favor). This phrase is used constantly in Korea, where splitting bills and paying back by instant transfer is the social norm — you ask for the other person's 계좌번호 and 이체 immediately. A complete transfer request also needs the bank name (은행 이름) and the account holder name (예금주 이름), since apps ask you to confirm the holder before sending. Three ways to request it: 알려 주세요 ('let me know', standard); 불러 주세요 ('read it aloud', when you'll type as they talk); 찍어 줘 ('text it to me', the casual message shorthand). Note the sharp contrast: 계좌번호 (account number, freely shared to receive money) vs 비밀번호 (PIN/password, never share). The English-speaker trap is using 가르쳐 주세요 — 가르치다 means 'to teach a skill', not 'to inform'; for giving information, the verb is 알리다 → 알려 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 계좌번호 ('account number') + 좀 (softener) + 알리다 → 알려 주세요 ('please inform/let me know'). A full account hand-off includes: bank name (국민은행) + number + 예금주 (account holder). Apps verify the holder's name before confirming a transfer.
알려 주세요 ('inform me', standard) vs 불러 주세요 ('read aloud', for dictating) vs 찍어 줘 ('text it over', casual). Key contrast: 계좌번호 (share freely to get paid) ≠ 비밀번호 (secret PIN, never share).
Formal to anyone: 계좌번호 좀 알려 주세요. With friends: 계좌번호 좀 알려 줘 / 계좌 찍어 줘 (반말 text). Giving yours humbly: 제 계좌번호 알려 드릴게요. Asking for all details at once: 계좌번호랑 예금주 성함 알려 주세요.

Used in everyday bill-splitting situations between friends (casual 알려 줘) and at a bank or with a colleague (polite 알려 주세요). Always 존댓말 when dealing with staff or someone senior. This phrase is never used with a teller — you give YOUR number to others, not ask for the bank's.

Using 가르쳐 주세요 — 가르치다 means 'to teach a skill'; sharing a piece of information uses 알리다: 계좌번호 알려 주세요. 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like asking for a lesson, not data. Also forgetting the 은행 name — the account number alone is insufficient for a transfer.

mistakes: Using 가르쳐 주세요 to ask for the number.
가르치다 = 'to teach (a skill)'. For sharing information like a number, use 알리다: 계좌번호 알려 주세요. 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like requesting instruction.
Confusing 계좌번호 with 비밀번호.
계좌번호 (account number) is shared so people can pay you; 비밀번호 (PIN/password) is secret. Never give your 비밀번호 to receive money — only your 계좌번호.
Forgetting to give the 은행 (bank name).
A 계좌번호 alone isn't enough — the sender needs the BANK too (예: 국민은행 123-45-6789). Say the 은행 first, then the number.

english: Please check if the deposit came in
usage: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요
Please check if it was deposited
Polite; asking a teller or person to confirm money arrived on your side
입금됐어요?
Did it come in? / Has it been deposited?
Quick direct check that a transfer has landed
아직 입금 안 됐는데요
It hasn't come in yet
What you say when the expected money is still missing
입금 확인되면 알려 주세요
Let me know once you confirm the deposit
Asking for a follow-up notification when it's confirmed
examples: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요.
Please check if the deposit came in.
Asking the teller to verify an incoming transfer; -는지 = 'whether'
A: 방금 보냈는데 입금됐어요? / B: 잠시만요. 네, 방금 들어왔어요.
A: I just sent it — did it come in? / B: One moment. Yes, it just came in.
A/B exchange: 보냈다 (sent — sender's side) vs 들어왔어요 ('came in' — receiver's side); 들어오다 is the vivid casual alternative to 입금되다; 잠시만요 is the polite bank-staff form
월급이 아직 입금 안 됐는데 언제 들어와요?
My salary hasn't come in yet — when will it arrive?
들어오다 ('to come in') is the casual spoken verb for money landing in an account
nuance: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요 is 입금 (入金, 'money in = deposit') + 되다 (passive 'be done') + -는지 ('whether') + 확인해 주세요 ('please check'). 입금 is the word for money ARRIVING in an account — the receiving side of any transfer. It pairs naturally with 송금/이체 (the sending side): the sender says 이체했어요 ('I sent it'), the receiver checks 입금됐어요? ('did it come in?'). A warmer, common alternative is 들어오다 ('to come in'): 돈 들어왔어요? and 월급 들어왔어요? are everyday spoken forms. The grammar point: 입금되다 (passive, money arrives on its own) vs 입금하다 (active, you deposit money) — 'did it arrive?' is passive 입금됐어요?, while 'I'll deposit it' is active 입금할게요. The -는지 structure makes an indirect question embedded in 확인해 주세요 and attaches to the verb stem (됐는지), not as a separate word. Casually: 입금됐어? or 돈 들어왔어?

structuredNuance.t: 입금 (入金, 'money in') + 되다 (passive) + -는지 ('whether') + 확인해 주세요 ('please check'). 입금 is the receiving side of a transfer. -는지 creates an embedded indirect question: it attaches to the verb stem (입금됐는지), not as a separate clause. Casual: 입금됐어? / 돈 들어왔어?

입금됐어요? (formal 'was it deposited?') vs 돈 들어왔어요? (casual 'did the money come in?'). Key grammar contrast: 입금되다 (passive, money arrives on its own) vs 입금하다 (active, you deposit). Use the passive to ask if money arrived; use the active when you're the one depositing.
입금 is 入金 — 入 'enter/in' + 金 'money'. Paired with 출금 (出金, 'money out = withdrawal'): 入 and 出 are the directional opposites that run through all banking vocabulary.
입금됐는지 확인해 주세요 is polite 존댓말 to a teller or someone you paid. Checking your own account informally: 입금됐어? or 돈 들어왔어? With salary: 월급 들어왔어? is what everyone says payday morning.

The passive/active confusion: 입금됐어요? (passive — did it arrive?) vs 입금했어요? (active — did you deposit it?). To ask if money has ARRIVED for you, use the passive 됐어요? If you accidentally use the active, you're asking if the other person did a manual deposit action, which is a different question.

mistakes: Mixing up 입금되다 and 입금하다.
입금되다 = 'be deposited / come in' (passive, money arrives): 입금됐어요?. 입금하다 = 'to deposit' (active, you put money in): 입금할게요. Use the passive for 'did it arrive'.
Confusing 입금 (in) with 출금 (out).
입금 (入金) is money coming IN; 출금 (出金) is money going OUT. 입금됐어요? asks if a deposit arrived; for a withdrawal you'd say 출금.
Saying 입금했는지 확인해 주세요 to check arrival.
That asks whether someone DEPOSITED (active). To check if money CAME IN, use the passive: 입금됐는지 확인해 주세요.

usage: 카드 정지시켜 주세요
Please freeze/block my card
Polite-urgent; 정지 (停止) = 'suspension/halt'; used when you notice the card missing
카드 분실 신고하려고요
I want to report my card lost
분실 신고 = 'loss report'; the formal procedure for a permanently lost/stolen card
카드 좀 막아 주세요
Please block my card
막다 ('to block/plug') — urgent spoken version people blurt at the call center
카드 재발급 받고 싶어요
I'd like a replacement card
재발급 = 'reissue' — the step you take after blocking to get a new card
examples: 카드 정지시켜 주세요.
Please freeze my card.
Said urgently at the bank when you can't find your card or suspect fraudulent use
A: 카드를 잃어버린 것 같아요. 정지시켜 주세요. / B: 네, 바로 정지하겠습니다. 재발급도 원하세요?
A: I think I lost my card. Please freeze it. / B: Of course, I'll suspend it right away. Would you also like a replacement?
Full urgent exchange: 정지 → B offers 재발급; B uses -하겠습니다 (bank staff's formal register)
일단 카드 막아 주시고, 재발급도 해 주세요.
First please block the card, then reissue it too.
일단 ('first of all') prioritizes the freeze before the replacement — natural two-step request
nuance: 카드 정지시켜 주세요 is 카드 + 정지 (停止, 'suspension/halt') + 시키다 (causative, 'cause to happen') + 주세요. This is high-stakes vocabulary — get it right. 정지(시키다) means to SUSPEND/freeze the card (potentially reversible); for a lost or stolen card you'll also 분실 신고하다 ('file a loss report'), which permanently blocks it so you then 재발급 ('reissue') a new one. The spoken urgent verb is 막다 ('to block/stop up') — 카드 막아 주세요 is what a panicked person blurts at the call center. The grammar point: 정지하다 (intransitive, 'the card stops') vs 정지시키다 (causative, 'cause it to be stopped') — when asking the bank to freeze YOUR card, 정지시켜 주세요 is the cleaner choice. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'cancel' as 취소하다 — 취소하다 cancels a transaction or reservation, NOT a card; a card is 정지/해지/분실 신고, never 취소. Also distinguish 정지 (temporary freeze, reversible) vs 해지 (permanent termination of the card/account). Always 존댓말 to staff in this situation.

structuredNuance.t: 카드 + 정지 (停止, 'stop/suspend') + 시키다 (causative, 'cause to happen') + 주세요. 정지 = temporary freeze (can be reversed); 분실 신고 = permanent block for lost/stolen cards; 재발급 = reissue a new card after blocking. The causative 시키다 is important: you're asking the bank to CAUSE the suspension.

카드 정지시키다 (formal, reversible suspend) vs 분실 신고하다 (formal procedure, permanently blocks for loss) vs 카드 막다 (spoken urgent 'block it'). Critical: 정지 (freeze, reversible) ≠ 해지 (terminate the card permanently). And: 취소하다 = cancel a transaction/reservation, NOT a card.
정지 is 停止 — 停 'stop/halt' + 止 'cease'. 분실 is 紛失 'loss/misplacement'. 재발급 is 再發給 're-issue/re-supply'.

Always 존댓말 — this is an urgent call-center or counter interaction. There is no casual version you'd realistically need; even with bank app chat support you use polite forms. Staff will respond in formal 합쇼체: 바로 정지하겠습니다.

Two traps: (1) using 취소하다 for 'cancel a card' — 취소 cancels a transaction/order, not a card; say 정지/해지/분실 신고. (2) using 정지하다 instead of 정지시키다 — 정지하다 can sound like 'the card stops on its own' (intransitive); the causative 시키다 makes your request clear: 'please MAKE it stop'.

mistakes: Saying 카드 취소해 주세요 to block a card.
취소하다 cancels a transaction/order/reservation, not a card. To block a card say 카드 정지시켜 주세요, or for a lost card 분실 신고하려고요.
Using 정지하다 instead of 정지시키다.
정지하다 can sound like the card itself stops. To request the bank CAUSE it to be suspended, the causative 정지시키다 is clearer: 카드 정지시켜 주세요.
Confusing 정지 (suspend) with 해지 (terminate).
정지 is a (possibly temporary) freeze; 해지 permanently terminates the card/account. If you only lost it and want a new one, you 정지/분실 신고 + 재발급, not 해지.

english: My card didn't work / got declined
usage: 카드가 안 됐어요
My card didn't go through
Polite; the general catch-all 'it didn't work' at a register — covers any failure
결제가 안 돼요
The payment won't go through
결제 ('payment/settlement') is the precise noun at checkout; used when the card itself is fine but payment fails
카드가 거절됐어요
My card was declined
거절되다 ('be rejected') — more explicit and formal, often mirrors error messages
한도 초과라고 떠요
It says 'limit exceeded'
한도 초과 = the exact on-screen error message you'll see for overspending
examples: 카드가 안 됐어요.
My card didn't work.
Said to the cashier when the terminal rejects the card; the all-purpose opening line
A: 결제가 계속 안 돼서요. 다시 한번 해 봐도 될까요? / B: 네, 카드 다시 대 주세요.
A: The payment keeps failing. Could we try one more time? / B: Sure, please tap the card again.
A/B exchange at a cashier: 결제가 안 되다 is the precise payment-failure framing; B asks to tap again (대다 = tap/present a card)
카드 정지돼서 그런지 결제가 자꾸 거절돼요.
Maybe because my card's frozen, payments keep getting declined.
정지돼서 그런지 ('maybe because it's frozen') — 그런지 expresses a tentative reason; 거절되다 is the more explicit 'declined'
nuance: 카드가 안 됐어요 is 카드 + 가 (subject particle) + 안 ('not') + 되다 ('to work/function') in past polite. 되다 is the workhorse verb for 'something functions/goes through', so 안 되다 ('doesn't work') is the first thing to say whenever a card fails — it covers a declined card, a frozen card, a dead chip, or a bad terminal. For more precision at checkout the noun is 결제 ('payment/settlement'): 결제가 안 돼요 ('the payment won't go through'). For an explicit 'declined', 거절되다 mirrors the error message. A common real cause is 한도 초과 ('limit exceeded'). Grammar trap: it must be 카드가 안 됐어요 (subject particle 가, past 됐), not 카드를 안 했어요 (object particle 를 means 'I didn't do the card' — nonsense). The English-speaker trap is translating 'work' as 일하다 ('to labor') — 카드가 일 안 해요 is wrong and confusing; a device 'working' is 되다, never 일하다. Also: 카드가 틀렸어요 ('the card is incorrect', like a wrong answer) is wrong for a declined card; use 안 됐어요. Casual: 카드 안 돼.

structuredNuance.t: 카드 + 가 (subject) + 안 ('not') + 되다 ('work/function'): 되다 is the Korean verb for 'something functions/goes through'. 안 되다 is the catch-all when a card fails for any reason. The past form 됐 → 안 됐어요 = 'didn't go through'. For an ongoing failure use the present: 카드가 안 돼요.

카드가 안 됐어요 (general 'didn't work', broadest) vs 결제가 안 돼요 ('payment fails', precise at a checkout) vs 거절됐어요 ('was declined', mirrors official error message). 한도 초과 = 'limit exceeded' (the specific cause if you've overspent).
Past (just happened): 카드가 안 됐어요. Present (still failing): 카드가 안 돼요. Guessing cause: 한도 초과인 것 같아요 ('I think it's over the limit'). Urgent re-try: 다시 한번 해 볼게요. Casual: 카드 안 돼.

Used with cashiers, tellers, or bank staff — always 존댓말. 되다/안 되다 is the appropriate register level: direct but polite. In casual chat with a friend you'd just say 카드 안 돼 or 카드 긁혔어? ('did the card go through?'). 긁히다 ('to be swiped') is the casual verb for a card transaction.

Two traps: (1) 일하다 for 'work' — 카드가 일 안 해요 is wrong and funny; a device/process working is 되다. (2) 틀리다 for a declined card — 틀리다 means 'to be incorrect (an answer)'; a non-functioning card is 안 되다 / 거절되다. Also: subject particle 가 (not object 를) is required.

mistakes: Translating 'work' as 일하다.
일하다 means 'to do labor/have a job'. A card/machine functioning is 되다: 카드가 안 됐어요. 카드가 일 안 해요 is incorrect.
Saying 카드를 안 했어요.
With 를 it means 'I didn't do the card'. The card is the SUBJECT of failing, so use 가: 카드가 안 됐어요.
Using 틀리다 for a declined card.
틀리다 = 'to be wrong/incorrect (an answer)'. A card that won't process is 안 되다 / 거절되다, not 틀리다. Say 카드가 안 됐어요.

usage: 환전하고 싶어요
I'd like to exchange currency
Polite; 환전 (換錢) is the standard word for currency exchange at a bank or 환전소
달러로 환전돼요?
Can I exchange into dollars?
Specifying the target currency with 로/으로 — direction particle for the result
환전하려고 하는데요
I'm here to exchange money
-는데요 softens and opens the conversation with the teller
오늘 환율 어떻게 돼요?
What's today's exchange rate?
환율 ('exchange rate') is the partner word you'll always ask about before committing
examples: 환전하고 싶어요.
I'd like to exchange money.
Said at a bank counter or 환전소 (dedicated exchange booth)
A: 원화를 달러로 환전하고 싶어요. / B: 오늘 환율이 얼마예요?
A: I'd like to exchange won into dollars. / B: What's today's exchange rate?
A/B exchange: A states currencies with A를 B로 pattern; B asks the rate before quoting
환율이 오늘 안 좋아서 조금만 환전할게요.
The rate's bad today, so I'll only exchange a little.
환율이 안 좋다 ('the rate is unfavorable') — the natural everyday collocation for judging whether to exchange
nuance: 환전하고 싶어요 is 환전 (換錢, 'exchange-money = currency exchange') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. Currency exchange is done at a bank or a 환전소 (dedicated booth, often better rates). The essential partner word is 환율 (換率, 'exchange rate') — ask 환율 어떻게 돼요? and judge with 환율이 좋다/안 좋다 ('the rate is good/bad'). To name currencies, use 로/으로 for the target: 달러로 환전하다 ('exchange INTO dollars'), 원화로 바꾸다. A plainer synonym is 바꾸다 ('change/swap') — 달러로 바꾸고 싶어요 is natural and slightly more colloquial. The critical confusion to avoid: 환전 (換錢, 'exchange money') vs 환불 (還拂, 'refund') — they look and sound similar but 환불 means getting your money back for a returned purchase; never say 환전 at a store return counter. Another trap: 교환하다 ('exchange goods, swap sizes') is for trading items, not currency. Also keep 환율 (the rate) distinct from 수수료 (the fee charged for the exchange), which is a separate cost worth asking about. To staff use 존댓말 throughout.

structuredNuance.t: 환전 (換錢, 'exchange-money') + 하다 + -고 싶어요. To specify what you exchange and into what, use A를 B로: 원화를 달러로 환전하다. The target currency takes 로/으로 (direction). Partner word: 환율 (exchange rate) — 환율이 좋다/안 좋다 to judge timing.

환전하다 (formal, standard) vs 바꾸다 (casual, 'change/swap'). Critical contrasts: 환전 (currency exchange) ≠ 환불 (refund for returned goods) ≠ 교환 (swapping goods/sizes). Use 환전 only for money-for-money conversion.
환전 is 換錢 — 換 'swap/exchange' + 錢 'money'. 환율 is 換率 — same 換 + 率 'rate/ratio'. 환불 is 還拂 — 還 'return' + 拂 'pay out': different 한자, different meaning.

Used at a bank or 환전소 — always 존댓말. With a currency exchange app or comparison website, you still use the same formal term 환전. Casual equivalent: 달러로 바꾸고 싶은데요. Asking about the rate first is culturally expected — exchange booths assume you'll ask before deciding.

Two traps: (1) confusing 환전 with 환불 — similar sound, opposite meanings; 환불 = refund, 환전 = currency swap. (2) marking the target currency with 에 — the direction particle is 로/으로: 달러로 환전하다, not 달러에 환전하다. Source uses 을/를: 원화를 달러로.

mistakes: Confusing 환전 (exchange money) with 환불 (refund).
환전 (換錢) = swap currency; 환불 (還拂) = refund a purchase. At a store you ask 환불, at a bank 환전. They're not interchangeable.
Using 교환하다 for currency.
교환하다 is exchanging GOODS (swap a size/item). Currency is 환전하다 or 바꾸다. 돈을 교환하다 sounds like bartering objects, not changing money.
Marking the target currency with 에.
The currency you change INTO takes 로/으로: 달러로 환전하다. 달러에 환전하다 is wrong. Source uses 을/를: 원화를 달러로.

usage: 환율 어떻게 돼요?
What's the exchange rate?
Polite-neutral; the idiomatic way to ask for a rate or numeric figure
오늘 달러 환율 얼마예요?
What's today's dollar rate?
얼마예요 ('how much') when you want the number directly and the currency is specified
환율 우대돼요?
Do I get a preferential rate?
환율 우대 = a preferred/discount rate banks offer to app users or regulars
지금 환율이 좋아요?
Is the rate good right now?
Asking whether it's a favorable time to exchange — 좋다/안 좋다 is the natural judgment phrase
examples: 환율 어떻게 돼요?
What's the exchange rate?
Asked at the bank or exchange booth before deciding how much to convert
A: 오늘 달러 환율 얼마예요? / B: 지금 1,350원이에요.
A: What's the dollar rate today? / B: Right now it's 1,350 won.
A/B exchange: 얼마예요? asks for the number; B gives the rate as 원 per 1 dollar — the standard Korean quote format
환율 우대 받으면 수수료가 좀 줄어요?
If I get a preferential rate, does the fee drop a bit?
환율 우대 ('rate preference') often bundles with a reduced 수수료 — worth asking together
nuance: 환율 어떻게 돼요? is 환율 (換率, 'exchange rate') + 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it come to be?'), the idiomatic Korean way to ask for a numeric figure or status. The construction 어떻게 돼요? is broadly useful — Koreans use it for rates, prices, totals, even your name (이름이 어떻게 되세요?) — and sounds more natural and polite than blunt 얼마예요? for abstract figures, though both work for 환율. A money-saving phrase: 환율 우대 ('preferential exchange rate') — banks and their apps give 우대 (優待, 'preferential treatment') to regulars or digital users, so asking 환율 우대 돼요? can get you a better deal. Don't confuse 환율 (the rate, a number) with 환전 (the act of exchanging). The English-speaker trap is calquing 'what is the exchange rate?' as 환율이 뭐예요? — but 뭐예요? asks 'what is it (by definition)?', so it sounds like you're asking the meaning of the term; use 어떻게 돼요? or 얼마예요? for the numeric value. Casual form with a friend: 환율 어떻게 돼?

structuredNuance.t: 환율 (換率, 'exchange rate') + 어떻게 돼요? ('how does it work out?'). 어떻게 돼요? is the idiomatic question for 'what is the value/status of X?' — also used for prices, totals, names. Both 어떻게 돼요? and 얼마예요? work for rates; the former is slightly softer and more natural. Casual: 환율 어떻게 돼?
환율 어떻게 돼요? (polite, for a figure/status) vs 환율 얼마예요? (direct, 'how much?'). Key vocabulary pair: 환율 (the rate, a number) vs 환전 (the act of exchanging). Don't confuse the rate with the transaction.
환율 is 換率 — 換 'swap/exchange' + 率 'rate/ratio'. 우대 in 환율 우대 is 優待 — 優 'preferential/excellent' + 待 'treatment': a better rate for valued customers.

Used at a bank, exchange booth, or app — always 존댓말 with staff. With friends discussing their recent trip: 환율 어떻게 됐어? is casual. Culturally, asking the rate before committing to an exchange is expected and shows savvy; follow up with 환율 우대 돼요? to potentially get a better deal.

Asking 환율이 뭐예요? — 뭐예요? asks 'what is it (by definition)?', sounding like you want an explanation of the term 'exchange rate'. For the numeric value, use 어떻게 돼요? or 얼마예요?. This is one of the most common awkward-phrasing errors at exchange booths.

mistakes: Asking 환율이 뭐예요? for the number.
뭐예요? asks 'what is it (by definition)?'. For a numeric rate use 환율 어떻게 돼요? or 환율 얼마예요?. 뭐예요? sounds like asking the meaning of the term.
Confusing 환율 with 환전.
환율 (換率) is the RATE (a number); 환전 (換錢) is the ACT of exchanging. You ask 환율 어떻게 돼요? then say 환전할게요 to do it.
Not knowing 우대 and missing a better rate.
환율 우대 ('preferential rate') is a real discount banks offer. Asking 환율 우대 돼요? can save money; without the word you may pay the full rate.

english: Please change this into smaller bills/coins
usage: 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요
Please break this into change
Polite; 잔돈 = 'small change/small bills'; the standard request to break a large bill
천 원짜리로 바꿔 주세요
Please change it into 1,000-won bills
Specify the denomination with 짜리 ('worth ~'); the most natural way to name a bill type
동전으로 좀 바꿔 주실 수 있어요?
Could you change this into coins?
동전 = 'coins' specifically; -주실 수 있어요 is extra polite for a slightly unusual request
만 원만 잔돈으로 주세요
Please give me 10,000 won in change
When you want only PART of an amount as small bills — 만 ('just/only') limits it
examples: 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요.
Please break this into change.
Handing a 50,000-won note over the counter and asking for smaller bills
A: 오만 원권을 만 원짜리로 바꿔 주세요. / B: 네, 오만 원 맞으시죠? 잠깐만요.
A: Please change this 50,000-won note into 10,000-won bills. / B: Right, that's 50,000 won? One moment.
Full exchange: 권 = large-denomination note; 짜리 = denomination you want; B confirms amount
동전이 필요한데 천 원만 동전으로 바꿔 주실 수 있어요?
I need coins — could you change just 1,000 won into coins?
Asking specifically for 동전 (coins) for a vending machine or coin locker; limiting amount with 만
nuance: 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요 is 잔돈 ('small change/change') + -으로 ('into') + 바꾸다 ('to change/swap') + 주세요. 잔돈 covers both small-denomination bills and coins, and is also the word for the change you get back after paying — though 거스름돈 is the more precise term for 'change returned by a cashier'. To specify the denomination you want, use -짜리 ('a thing worth ~'): 천 원짜리 ('a 1,000-won bill'), 만 원짜리 ('a 10,000-won bill'). For coins specifically say 동전. The verb 바꾸다 ('to swap/change') is the same one used casually for currency exchange — context tells the listener you mean breaking a bill. The particle trap: it's 잔돈으로 바꾸다 (target marked with 으로 = 'change INTO small bills'), not 잔돈을 바꾸다 (which would mean 'change the small bills themselves'). Confusing 잔돈 (physical small cash) with 잔액 (account balance figure) is a real learner mix-up despite both having 잔 (殘, 'remaining'). Casual: 잔돈으로 바꿔 줘.

structuredNuance.t: 잔돈 ('small change') + -으로 ('into', direction particle) + 바꾸다 ('to swap/change') + 주세요. -으로 marks the target form (what you want it changed INTO). To name the denomination: -짜리 (천 원짜리 = 1,000-won bill). For coins: 동전. Casual: 잔돈으로 바꿔 줘.

잔돈 ('small bills and coins, change') vs 거스름돈 ('change returned by a cashier') — 잔돈 is the broader term; 거스름돈 specifically means the change a seller gives back. Also: 잔돈 (physical small cash) ≠ 잔액 (account balance figure) — both use 잔 (殘) but are completely different.
Generic: 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요. Named denomination: 천 원짜리로 바꿔 주세요. Coins only: 동전으로 바꿔 주세요. Partial: 만 원만 잔돈으로 주세요. If the cashier forgets your change: 거스름돈요 ('my change, please').

Used with bank tellers, cashiers, or convenience store staff — polite 존댓말 is standard. Breaking a bill is a routine, unawkward request in Korea. With a friend you'd ask 잔돈으로 바꿔 줄 수 있어? Denomination names use native Korean numbers + 원짜리 (천 원짜리, 오천 원짜리).

The particle: it's 잔돈으로 바꾸다 ('change INTO small bills', target takes 으로), not 잔돈을 바꾸다 ('change the small bills', which means something different). Also: confusing 잔돈 (cash in hand) with 잔액 (balance in account) — both share 잔 (殘) but refer to entirely different things.

mistakes: Marking the target with 을 instead of 으로.
You change money INTO small bills: 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요 (으로 = 'into'). 잔돈을 바꾸다 would mean 'change the small money itself'.
Confusing 잔돈 with 잔액.
잔돈 = physical small change/bills; 잔액 = your account balance (a number). Both have 잔, but ask 잔돈으로 바꿔 주세요 for cash, 잔액 확인 for the balance.
Using -원 instead of -원짜리 for a denomination.
To name a bill type, use 짜리 ('worth'): 천 원짜리 ('a 1,000-won note'). Bare 천 원 is just the amount; 천 원짜리로 specifies the bill you want.

usage: 통장 정리 좀 해 주세요
Could you update my bankbook?
Polite; 통장 정리 = printing recent transactions into the physical passbook
거래 내역 좀 뽑아 주세요
Please print out my transaction history
거래 내역 = 'transaction record'; 뽑다 ('to print/pull') — for a paper statement
통장 정리하려고요
I'm here to update my passbook
Stating your purpose at the counter or the self-service 통장정리기 machine
입출금 내역 좀 볼 수 있어요?
Can I see my deposit/withdrawal history?
입출금 내역 = the full deposit-and-withdrawal list; 볼 수 있어요? for viewing on screen
examples: 통장 정리 좀 해 주세요.
Could you update my bankbook, please?
Handing the passbook to a teller, or walking up to the self-service 통장정리기 machine
A: 통장 정리하려고 하는데 기계 어디 있어요? / B: 저 안쪽에 통장정리기 있어요.
A: I want to update my passbook — where's the machine? / B: The passbook machine is further inside.
A/B at the branch: 통장정리기 is the self-service machine; B directs you in
지난달 거래 내역 좀 뽑아 주시겠어요?
Could you print last month's transaction history?
거래 내역 ('transaction history') is the right term for a paper statement of past activity; 뽑다 = 'print/pull out'
nuance: 통장 정리 좀 해 주세요 is 통장 ('bankbook/passbook') + 정리 (整理, 'tidying/sorting') + 좀 + 해 주세요. 통장 정리 is a distinctly Korean banking ritual — feeding your physical passbook into a 통장정리기 (self-service machine) or handing it to a teller to PRINT the latest transactions into it. Here 정리 means 'putting the records in order', NOT its common meaning of 'cleaning up/throwing away'. This distinction matters: if someone hears 정리 and thinks 'dispose of', 통장 정리해 주세요 might sound like 'close my account' — but it does NOT. To close an account, you'd say 통장 해지 / 계좌 해지 ('terminate'). For a broader printed statement, ask for 거래 내역 (transaction history) or 입출금 내역 (deposit/withdrawal history), which you 뽑다 ('print/pull') or 출력하다. Korea still uses physical passbooks, making this a common real-world request. Another key distinction: 통장 (the physical passbook) vs 계좌 (the account, a number in the banking system) — you do 정리 on the 통장, but funds and balances live in the 계좌. Casually: 통장 정리 좀 해 줘 with a teller you know, but 존댓말 is the norm.

structuredNuance.t: 통장 ('bankbook') + 정리 (整理, 'put in order') + 좀 + 해 주세요. 정리 here = printing recent transactions into the passbook, NOT 'tidying/disposing'. It's a specific action: you feed the book into the 통장정리기 machine or hand it to a teller to print the entries.

통장 정리 (print entries into the passbook) vs 거래 내역 뽑다 (print a separate paper statement). Critical contrast: 통장 정리 ≠ 통장 해지 (terminating/closing the account). Don't let 정리 ('tidy up') make you think the account is being closed.
정리 is 整理 — 整 'put in order/tidy' + 理 'manage/reason'. 해지 is 解止 — 解 'dissolve' + 止 'stop': actual termination of the account.

Always 존댓말 at a bank branch. This phrase is routine and polite. Many branches now have self-service 통장정리기 machines — you just feed the book in. If you need an older-style teller update, this phrase is exactly what to say at the counter.

Reading 정리 as 'tidy up/dispose of' and worrying 통장 정리 means closing the account — it doesn't. 정리 here means updating the record. To CLOSE an account say 계좌 해지. Also: assuming Korean banking is entirely digital — physical passbooks (통장) are still in regular use and 통장 정리 is a real, common request.

mistakes: Reading 정리 as 'close/clear out' the account.
통장 정리 means PRINTING recent transactions into the passbook, not closing it. To close an account, say 통장 해지 / 계좌 해지. 정리 ≠ termination.
Confusing 통장 with 계좌.
통장 is the physical passbook; 계좌 is the account (number/funds). You 통장 정리 (update the book), but transfers and balances refer to the 계좌.
Saying 통장 내역 for a printed statement.
The standard term is 거래 내역 or 입출금 내역 ('transaction/deposit-withdrawal history'). 통장 정리 updates the book; 거래 내역 뽑다 prints a statement.

english: I'd like to set up an automatic payment/transfer
usage: 자동이체 신청하고 싶어요
I'd like to set up auto-transfer
Polite; 자동이체 = recurring automatic account debit; 신청하다 = apply/sign up for
자동이체 걸어 놨어요
I've set it on auto-pay
걸어 놓다 ('to set/hook up and leave') — the natural spoken phrase for arranging auto-debit
자동이체 날짜 바꾸고 싶어요
I'd like to change the auto-debit date
Adjusting which day of the month the recurring payment is pulled
자동이체 해지하려고요
I want to cancel the auto-transfer
해지하다 ('to terminate') a standing recurring instruction — not 취소, which is for one-off transactions
examples: 자동이체 신청하고 싶어요.
I'd like to set up an automatic transfer.
Said to a teller to arrange recurring rent or utility payments
A: 월세 자동이체 걸어 놓으면 매달 빠져나가요? / B: 네, 지정한 날짜에 자동으로 빠져나가요.
A: If I set up auto-pay for rent, does it come out monthly? / B: Yes, it comes out automatically on the designated date.
Full A/B exchange: 걸어 놓다 for 'set it up'; 빠져나가다 ('slip out') is the vivid native verb for money being pulled from an account
통신비는 자동이체로 해 놨는데 날짜 좀 바꿔 주세요.
I've got my phone bill on auto-pay — please change the date.
자동이체로 해 놓다 ('have it set to auto') — the -아/어 놓다 pattern for a state you've left in place
nuance: 자동이체 신청하고 싶어요 is 자동 (自動, 'automatic') + 이체 ('transfer') + 신청하다 ('to apply for / sign up') + -고 싶어요. 자동이체 is the recurring auto-debit set up for rent (월세), utilities (공과금), phone bills (통신비), and subscriptions — essential for life in Korea, where most regular bills are pulled automatically from your bank account. Formally you 신청하다 ('apply for') the arrangement at a bank; colloquially people say 자동이체 걸어 놓다 / 해 놓다 ('set it up and leave it running'), using the -아/어 놓다 pattern for a maintained state. The vivid verb for money being auto-deducted is 빠져나가다 ('to slip out/be drawn out'): 돈이 빠져나가요. To stop it, you 해지하다 ('terminate'), not 취소하다 — 취소 is for one-off transactions, 해지 is for standing instructions. Key contrast: 자동이체 (recurring account-to-account debit) vs 자동 결제 (card-based auto-charge for subscriptions) — they overlap but 이체 is account debit, 결제 is card charge. Also: 신청 (you apply) vs 접수 (the bank receives/registers your application) — you 신청, the bank 접수. Always 존댓말 with staff.

structuredNuance.t: 자동 (自動, 'automatic') + 이체 ('transfer') + 신청하다 ('to apply for') + -고 싶어요. 자동이체 = recurring auto-debit from a bank account (rent, utilities, phone bill). Colloquial setup verb: 걸어 놓다 / 해 놓다 ('set it up and leave it'). Money leaving: 빠져나가다 ('slip out').

자동이체 (recurring account debit, 이체 = bank transfer) vs 자동 결제 (card-based auto-charge for subscriptions, 결제 = payment). For bank debits (rent, utilities): 자동이체. For subscription cards (Netflix, etc.): 자동 결제. Also: 신청 (you apply) vs 접수 (bank receives it).
자동 is 自動 — 自 'self' + 動 'move': moves by itself. 신청 is 申請 — 申 'state/declare' + 請 'request'. 해지 is 解止 — 解 'dissolve' + 止 'stop': permanently terminating a standing arrangement.

Always 존댓말 at a bank counter or call center. In app menus you tap 자동이체 신청/해지 as labels. With a friend: 자동이체 해 놨어? is casual. The -아/어 놓다 pattern (걸어 놓다, 해 놓다) is very natural in spoken Korean and marks a persistent state.

Using 취소하다 to stop a recurring auto-transfer — 취소 cancels a one-off transaction or order; to end a standing auto-debit arrangement use 해지하다: 자동이체 해지하려고요. Also confusing 자동이체 (bank account debit) with 자동 결제 (card charge) — different systems, different cancellation processes.

mistakes: Confusing 자동이체 with 자동 결제.
자동이체 is recurring account-to-account debit (rent, utilities); 자동 결제 is card-based auto-charge (subscriptions). Ask for 자동이체 for bank debits, 자동 결제 for card subscriptions.
Using 취소하다 to stop a standing auto-transfer.
취소하다 cancels a one-off transaction. To END a recurring instruction, use 해지하다: 자동이체 해지하려고요. 취소 is for a single payment, not the whole arrangement.
Saying 신청 when you mean to ask the bank's confirmation.
신청하다 = YOU apply/sign up. The bank's side of receiving it is 접수. Say 자동이체 신청하고 싶어요 to request setup; the bank then 접수 (processes) it.

Is there an ATM nearby?
Polite-neutral; asking a passerby or staff where to find a machine
여기 현금인출기 어디 있어요?
Where's the cash machine here?
현금인출기 ('cash withdrawal machine') is the full native Korean term for ATM
이 카드 여기서 돼요?

Checking your specific card is accepted at this particular machine
편의점에 ATM 있나요?
Is there an ATM in the convenience store?
Convenience-store ATMs (편의점) are ubiquitous but almost always charge a 수수료
examples: 혹시 근처에 ATM 있어요?
Is there an ATM nearby, by any chance?
혹시 ('by any chance') softens asking a stranger on the street — essential polite opener
A: 현금인출기 어디 있어요? 돈 좀 뽑으려고요. / B: 저 편의점 안에 있어요.
A: Where's the ATM? I need to take out some cash. / B: It's inside that convenience store.
A/B on the street: pair the location question with the purpose (돈 뽑으려고요); B points you to the 편의점
이 ATM 다른 은행 카드도 돼요?
Does this ATM take other banks' cards too?

nuance: 근처에 ATM 있어요? is 근처 ('vicinity/nearby') + 에 (location particle for existence) + ATM + 있어요? ('is there?'). Koreans say the English initialism ATM (pronounced 에이티엠) naturally, but the native term is 현금인출기 (現金引出機, 'cash withdrawal machine') or 자동화기기 (the bank's signage term for an all-in-one deposit/withdraw kiosk) — all three are understood. The particle is the crunch point: a place where something EXISTS takes 에 (근처에 있어요?), while a place where an ACTION happens takes 에서 (ATM에서 돈을 뽑다, 'withdraw AT the ATM'). Using 에서 for 'is there an ATM' is the most common particle error here. Practically, ATMs are in bank lobbies (24-hour 365코너), convenience stores (편의점), and subway stations — but convenience-store and other-bank machines almost always charge a 수수료, and some bank ATMs restrict free service after hours. Always worth also asking 이 카드 여기서 돼요? to confirm your card works, and 외국 카드 돼요? for overseas cards. The English-speaker trap beyond particles: assuming all ATMs accept all cards — ask 다른 은행 카드도 돼요? or look for a 'Global ATM' sign for foreign cards. Casual form: 근처에 ATM 있어?

structuredNuance.t: 근처 ('nearby') + 에 (existence-location particle) + ATM + 있어요? ('is there?'). The particle is everything: 있다/없다 (existence) always takes 에, not 에서. 근처에 ATM 있어요? = 'Does an ATM exist near here?' Casual: 근처에 ATM 있어?

ATM (에이티엠, common loanword) = 현금인출기 (native full term) = 자동화기기 (bank signage term). All three are understood; 에이티엠 is the one people actually say on the street. Key particle contrast: 근처에 ATM 있어요? (존재, 에) vs ATM에서 돈을 뽑다 (행동 장소, 에서).
현금인출기 is 現金引出機 — 現金 'cash' + 引出 'draw out' + 機 'machine'. 자동화기기 is 自動化機器 — automated machine, the official bank term for the multi-function kiosk.

Used with strangers on the street (혹시 softens it) or in a shop/building. Add 혹시 when asking someone you don't know — it signals 'sorry to bother you' and is essential street courtesy. With a friend just say 근처에 ATM 있어? No 반말 with strangers.

Two traps: (1) 에 vs 에서 — existence takes 에 (근처에 있어요?), action location takes 에서 (ATM에서 뽑다). (2) Assuming all ATMs take all cards — other-bank and foreign-card support varies; ask 이 카드 여기서 돼요? / 외국 카드 돼요? before inserting.

mistakes: Using 에서 instead of 에 for existence.
Existence (있다/없다) takes 에: 근처에 ATM 있어요?. 에서 marks where an action occurs (ATM에서 뽑다, 'withdraw at the ATM'). For 'is there an ATM', use 에.
Assuming every ATM takes your (or a foreign) card.
Other-bank and convenience-store ATMs often charge fees, and not all accept foreign cards. Ask 이 카드 여기서 돼요? or 다른 은행 카드도 돼요?, and look for a Global ATM for overseas cards.
Saying 인출기 alone and expecting clarity.
The full word is 현금인출기 (cash withdrawal machine) or just ATM. Bare 인출기 is understood but incomplete; 현금인출기 or 에이티엠 is what people actually say.

usage: 이체 한도 좀 올려 주세요
Please raise my transfer limit
Polite; 한도 (限度) = 'permitted cap/ceiling', 올리다 ('to raise/increase')
1회 이체 한도가 얼마예요?
What's the per-transfer limit?
1회 ('per occurrence/per transaction') vs 1일 ('per day') — different caps, both matter
한도 초과라고 떠서 송금이 안 돼요
It says 'limit exceeded' so I can't send
한도 초과 = the exact on-screen error that blocks a transfer above your cap
출금 한도도 같이 올릴 수 있어요?
Can I raise the withdrawal limit too?
출금 한도 (withdrawal cap) is separate from the transfer cap — ask about both
examples: 이체 한도 좀 올려 주세요.
Please raise my transfer limit.
Said to a teller when you need to send an amount larger than your current cap allows
A: 한도 초과라고 떠서 이체가 안 돼요. 한도 올려 주세요. / B: 보안카드나 OTP 가져오셨어요?
A: It says limit exceeded so I can't transfer. Please raise the limit. / B: Did you bring your security card or OTP?
A/B at the counter: 한도 초과 as the triggering error; B asks for identity verification (보안카드/OTP) — required to raise limits
보안카드 없이는 한도를 못 올린다고요?
You're saying I can't raise the limit without a security card?
Quote the teller's statement back as an indirect question — 못 올린다고요? checks you understood correctly
nuance: 이체 한도 좀 올려 주세요 is 이체 ('transfer') + 한도 (限度, 'permitted ceiling/quota') + 좀 + 올리다 ('to raise') + 주세요. Korea sets surprisingly low default transfer limits — especially for new or foreigner accounts — split into 1회 한도 (per-transaction) and 1일 한도 (daily total), plus separate 출금 한도 (withdrawal cap) and 이체 한도 (transfer cap). New residents and foreigners constantly hit these, making 한도 올려 주세요 one of the most practically necessary phrases, usually requiring re-verification with a 보안카드 (security card) or OTP device. Natural verb pair: 올리다 ('raise') / 내리다 ('lower'). The blocking error is 한도 초과 ('exceeded the cap'). English-speaker trap: 한도 (permitted maximum/quota) vs 한계 (limit of ability or endurance, e.g. 체력의 한계 'physical limits') — you say 이체 한도, never 이체 한계. Another trap: 올리다 is the correct verb for raising a numeric cap; 늘리다 ('to increase/expand in size') is also acceptable but 올리다/높이다 ('raise/make higher') is more idiomatic for limits. Don't confuse 한도 (the permitted cap) with 잔액 (your actual balance) — a low 한도 can block a transfer even when your 잔액 is ample. Always 존댓말 to staff.

structuredNuance.t: 이체 ('transfer') + 한도 (限度, 'permitted ceiling') + 좀 + 올리다 ('raise') + 주세요. 한도 is the cap on how much you can move at once or per day. Korea defaults to low caps for new accounts — foreigners especially hit these. The error you'll see: 한도 초과 ('limit exceeded').

한도 (permitted maximum/quota) vs 한계 (boundary of ability/endurance: 체력의 한계). For a bank transfer cap, always 한도. Verb: 올리다/높이다 ('raise a cap') — standard. Also: 한도 (cap) ≠ 잔액 (actual balance) — you can have money but be blocked by a low 한도.
한도 is 限度 — 限 'limit/restrict' + 度 'degree/extent'. 초과 (in 한도 초과) is 超過 — 超 'exceed' + 過 'pass by/over'. Together: 'exceeded the permitted degree'.

Always 존댓말 at a bank counter or call center. Raising limits requires in-person verification with ID + 보안카드 or OTP. If at a call center, they'll walk you through the same verification. Keep 올려 주세요 as the core request; you can add urgency with 급하게 보내야 해서요 ('I urgently need to send it').

Using 한계 for a bank cap — 한계 = limit of endurance/ability (e.g. 'I've hit my limits'), not a numeric banking quota. Always use 한도 for transfer and withdrawal caps. Also: 크게 하다 ('make it big') for a numeric limit sounds wrong — the idiomatic verb is 올리다/높이다 ('raise it').

mistakes: Using 한계 instead of 한도 for an account cap.
한도 (限度) is a permitted maximum/quota (이체 한도). 한계 is a limit of ability/endurance (체력의 한계). For a transfer or withdrawal cap, always 한도.
Confusing 한도 (cap) with 잔액 (balance).
한도 is the MAX you're allowed to move; 잔액 is how much money you actually have. You can be blocked by a low 한도 even with a high 잔액. They're different problems.
Saying 한도 크게 해 주세요.
The idiomatic verb for a cap is 올리다/높이다 ('raise'): 한도 좀 올려 주세요. 크게 하다 ('make it big') sounds off for a numeric limit.
